summary: This memo extends NNTP so a client and server can use Transport Layer Security. The main goal is encrypting a single link for confidentiality, with data integrity, optional certificate-based authentication and optional compression also possible. It was later updated by RFC 8143 and RFC 8996.

plainLanguage.summary: STARTTLS lets an NNTP client and server begin with a normal connection and then switch to TLS on that same connection. After the TLS handshake, they start a fresh NNTP session over the protected link.

questions: how to use tls with nntp
subtitle: How an NNTP client upgrades a connection to TLS with the STARTTLS command.

tldr.problem: NNTP can send passwords and articles over an unencrypted connection, and using a separate port for TLS has drawbacks.
tldr.mechanism: The server advertises STARTTLS; the client sends the command, receives response 382, and begins TLS negotiation on the existing connection.
tldr.outcome: STARTTLS protects one client-server link, not an entire chain of NNTP servers. RFC 4642 was updated by RFC 8143 and RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4642 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2006 and was updated by RFC 8143 and RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why NNTP Uses TLS
sections.content:
The Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) moves news articles between clients and servers. An unencrypted connection exposes passwords and can be unsuitable when integrity or confidentiality is needed.

RFC 4642 formalizes the STARTTLS command, which was already used by some implementations. The RFC prefers this approach over starting TLS immediately on a dedicated TCP port.
sections.plainLanguage: Without TLS, someone on the network may read or alter NNTP traffic. STARTTLS lets the client request protection on the existing connection.

sections.title: Advertising STARTTLS
sections.content:
A server that supports the extension includes the STARTTLS capability in its response to CAPABILITIES. It must not advertise this capability after TLS is active or after successful authentication.

Because the capability affects security, the client must not rely on a cached capability list from an earlier session.
sections.plainLanguage: The server advertises STARTTLS when the command is available. The client checks the current connection instead of trusting an old capability list.

sections.title: Starting the TLS Handshake
sections.content:
The client sends STARTTLS as a separate command; it MUST NOT be pipelined. Response 382 means to begin TLS negotiation, 502 means the command is unavailable, and 580 means the server cannot start negotiation.

After response 382, the client MUST start TLS before sending another NNTP command. Negotiation begins with the first octet after the response's CRLF. If the handshake fails, both sides SHOULD close the connection.

After a successful handshake, the NNTP session resets to its state just after the greeting. The server discards pre-TLS knowledge about the client, and the client must not rely on the server's pre-TLS capability list.
sections.plainLanguage: After the server replies 382, the client starts TLS before sending anything else. Once TLS succeeds, both sides discard session information learned before the handshake.

sections.title: A Successful STARTTLS Exchange
sections.content:
The RFC example begins with the client requesting capabilities. The server lists STARTTLS. The client tries to select a restricted newsgroup and receives response 483, which says encryption or stronger authentication is required.

The client sends STARTTLS, receives 382 and completes TLS negotiation. It asks for capabilities again, then repeats the group request successfully. A later attempt to start TLS again receives 502 because a TLS layer is already active.
sections.plainLanguage: The client first learns that TLS is available. After switching to TLS, it checks capabilities again and retries the command that needed a secure connection.

sections.title: Security and Scope of Protection
sections.content:
Traffic before the TLS handshake is sent in the clear and can be changed by an active attacker. Both sides must discard sensitive knowledge from that period and should request capabilities again after TLS starts.

The protection covers a single NNTP link. Encrypting one connection does not protect an article across every server that later handles it. The client must also check that the server certificate matches the hostname used to open the connection.

An attacker could remove the STARTTLS capability from a capability reply to prevent a client from trying TLS. The RFC suggests remembering that a server previously offered TLS and warning if it disappears unexpectedly.
sections.plainLanguage: TLS protects only the connection between these two endpoints. Check the server's certificate name, and be alert if a server that used to offer TLS stops advertising it.
